It is yet uncertain whether M. Guizot will be able to retain his position as Minister of France. The discussion on the address to the Throne, was brought to a close in the Chamber of Feers, on Saturday the 18th ult. The number of members who baMolted were 153. and the ministerial majority was 73. 'I bis vote in favor of the picsent Cabinet is ascribed to the ( fleet produced bv a triumphant speech of the Duke de Broglie. The real struggle was to commence in the Chamber of Deputies on the 20th ult. and the

coming conflict had paralysed all movement on the Bourse þÿ what tended also lo excite alarm among the specoJalois, was a pma. graph which appeared rw La Fresse staling that the British Minister at Washington had demanded his passports. A deputation had waited on Admiral Dupetit Thouars, to solicit his acceptance of ihe sword of honor which had been subscribed for him by his friends and admirers, but the gallant Admiral fiankly declined it, on the ground that he could not do so consistently with his sense of duty. A loan of £1,500,000, is in course of negociation at London, for the St. Domingo Goveminent; the rate of interest being 5 per cent, payable there. It is conjectured the amount will be raised without the slightest difficulty. Queen Victoria has paid a visit to the Great Captain of tfie age at Sti atfieldsav e, the visit is ol an entirely private character and the particulars can afford but little imere-t to the general reader. The Peerage of the Governor General of Canada, Sir Charles Metcalfe has been gazetted. Sheridan Knowles is at Funchal delivering lectures on dramatic poetry : we trust he will be induced to visit the West India islands : among them St. Thomas. The report ot the death of the Emperor of Russia has been þÿcontradicted and the public mind is again at ease on the subject. The leading members of the tea trade m London held a meeting at the Jerusalem Collee house on the 18th ult. when it was determined to adof a reduction ol the duty upon that arti f dress a memorial to the government in favor .
Positive intelligence has been received that Dr. Wolff who has arrived at Teheran, from Bokhara, will return to England by way ol Russia and St. Pelersbuig.

EARTHQUAKE. Yesterday at 2 a, m. a severe shock of Earthquake was felt, which aroused a great portion ol the inhabitants from their slumbers. The noise was dreadful. We have not heard ol any damage being done, but these repeated shocks are truly alarming, as they lead us to infer that violent intestine commotions are still rile in this hemisphere. May the giver of all good ! protect not only us but the inhabitants of the whole of the West India islands from any awful visitation. þÿ Verily we may truly say, with the inspired writer. A Romantic Story þÿ A Swiss journal furnishes us with the following romantic tale of real life: þÿ A married couple, who had for several years lived in a state of anti-conjugal harmony, determined to part, and made an appointment with eaeh other to meet at a notary's to sign the deed of separation. To arrive at the office of the man of þÿlaw , they had to cross a lake, and, as it happened, they both embarked in the same boat. On their passage a storm arose, and the boat was upset. The htlsband, being a good swimmer, soon reached the shore in safety ; on looking around him to see the fate of tiis fellow passengers. he discovered his wife still struggling for her life, but in imminent danger. A feel ing of his earlv affection returned to him. and, plunging again into the water, he swam to her, and Succeeded in rescuing her. When she recovered her senses, and iearnt to whom she owed her life, she tluew h-rself into his arms He embraced her with equal cordiality, and they vowed an oblivion of all their differences, and that they would live and die together.

Woman's TemPeH þÿ No trait of character is more valuable in a female than the possession of a sweet temper. Home can never be rntide happy without it. It is like the flowers that spring up in our pathway, reviving ami cheering us. Let a man go home at night, wearied and worn bv the toils of the day, ami how soothing is a word dictated by a good disposition. ft is a sunshine falling upon his heart. He is happy, ami the cares of life are forgotten. A sweet temper has a soothing influence over tile minds of a whole family- Where it is found in the wife and mother, rnu mnv observe kindness and love predominating over the bad feeling of a natural heart. Smiles, kind words ami looks characterize the children, and peace and love have their dwelling there. Study to acquire and retain a sweet temper. It is more valuable than gold, it captivates more than beautv, and to the close ot life retains all its freshness and power.

Habits of tiii: Talegalla þÿ The Talegai (an la Australian bird, somewhat resembling our domestic fowl) does not hatch its eggs by incubation. In order to effect this object it assimilates, in some degree, to the practice of the ostrich, yet upon a totally different prin ,:jplo. The talegnlla collects together ms immense quantity of decavit g vegetable matter as a depository for the eggs, and then trusts to the heat engendered by the process of decomposition for the hatching them The heap employed for this purpose is collected by the birds during several weeks previously to the period of laying ; it varies in size from two to four cart loads, and is of a true pyramidal form. The construction of the mound is not the work of one pair of birdf but it is effected by the united labours of several ; the same site appears to tie resorted lo for several years in succession, the birds adding a fresh supply ol materials on each occasion previous to laying their eggs.

St. Thomas Times, 15th February. 1845 l ire in Barbadoes. Destructive Conflagration. We have been obliged by Captain Mc'lulosh of the brig Lady Campbell with a number of the Earbadoes Clobe of the bib inst., and it is with profound sorrow that we peruse an account of the terrible calamity which lias befallen Bridgetown. Barbadoes would appear to be singularly unfortunate, for on the night of the Urd and morning of the 4th Febv. a terrible calamity visiied the devoted city. A fourth of the stone built portion of the city is in ruins. Hundreds of the inhabitants without homes, clothes, or furniture. and thousands upon thousands of pounds worth of property has been destroyed by the devouring element. It appears that about five minutes belore nine o'clock on Monday night the fire broke out in Tudor street in a house belonging to Mr. Jacob Lewis from whence it spread in almost every direction notwithstanding the almost superhuman efforts to arrest its progress. The crews of H. B. M ships the Illustrious the Pique, and the liose sloop of war did all in their power to arrest the progress of the devouring element. All business in the city was still quite suspended, the stores closed, and every one's thoughts engrossed by the terrible calamity. The master and passengers of the Maid of Er in which arrived on the following morning from Grenada, described the appearance of the conflagration as seen by them fifty miles at sea. t<> have exhibited a spectacle of fearful sublimity. The total estimated loss of property is stated to be about £400,000 sterling For
179 large stores and dwellings are down. EUROPEAN HSTFHLt.RF.lSCE IN A M ERIC AN A t FAIRS.

The N. Y. Sun ot the 18th ult. contains an able leader under the above attractive heading, and as it purports to be a new view of the question ol Texan Annexation it cannot be perused without interest. The writer asserts that a grand scheme has been devised by that far-seeing monarch Louis Fhiltpje to found an empire on the American continent which will embrace the Brazils, and the intermediate countries, together with Mexico, under his son the l'rince de Joinvi'le and give him also the control of the isthmus of Panama, and the Pacific and the Atlantic. France lie continues, is opposed to Annexation. for she intends that the Mexican Empire shall extend to the Sabine. So that instead of Texas being independent, we may expect to have at no distant day Marshal Bogeaud, and the French army on our borders, as soon as they can be spared from Algiers. Strange as the above may seem, it is certain that the Bourhons (prior to the French revolution) actually concocted and seriously determined on prosecuting a plan precisely similar. France has been actively at work in Mexico, in bringing about the present revolution, and if Santa Anna is in reality deposed and his military rule swept to the winds, her interests will he materially strengthened. Brazil is also in a stale of revolution and the position of the present Emperor precarious in the extreme; he will therefore lie anxious to aid his brother iu law .n establish-

ing a new Empire in Mexico, and secure to himself the co operation of the French na/al and military power. Mexico, Columbia, Central America and the Brazils would form an Empire whix:h would rival in extent and value the Anglo Indian possessions. þÿ Ibid February 12.

ALARMING MORTALITY AMONG 'THE FISH ON THE COAST OF A M ERICA. We notice in the American papers that the shores of Long island, New Jersey and Delaware are lined with millions of dead fish, while thousands are found floating in every direction. The cause of this strange Phenomenon is yet unexplained The water in the infected district is of a dark brown, and immediately the fish enter it they are seized with convulsions, rise to the surface and die in a few minutes. Considerable dread exists that 011 tiie approach ol the summer, a posti lonce may arise from the immense masses of fish already thrown upon the coast The only feasible way we can account for this distressing calamity is that the sea in that district has been poisoned by an eruption of some sub marine volcano, and become thereby surcharged with pestilencial gas-es fatal to the existence of the scaly tribe The worst feature of this strange story is that by the latest accounts the mortality was spieading with fearful rapidity. þÿ Ibid

For example þÿ anil we state facts þÿ the Presidential election in Pennsylvania is on the first Friday in November: in New Yoik the Tuesday after the first Monday in Nov. ember. The intermediate days between holding the election in these two great Stales are full of intrigue and management. Bets to a large amount are made : Clubs, Committeemen, and special Deputations, are sent to the State last holding the election, having the returns from the other State If winning or losing the vote of that State is to decide (lie great question, any sunt of money is expended to serine the point, and it is generally carried by corruption. Apprehension and Kxecution of Ztirliano. The following particulars of the arrest and execution ot the brigand, together with a brief outline of his wicked caieer, ure furnished by the Spanish þÿpapers: Alter making an unsuccessful effort to escape in the direction of Portugal, Zarbano and his brother in- law, Cuyatano Muro, retraced their weary steps towards the rugged Cameros mountains, where they hoped to be able to lie concealed until the ardour of the þÿenemy p s ursuit relaxed, and the vigilance of the royal troops became lulled. After wan during for some days in the detiles of the Cameros, cold and hunger compelled the fugitives to seek the abodes of men, and one night Gay a ta no Muro managed to enter the village of Montenegro, and obtained, at the peril of his life, an interview with his wife, who confided his perilous condition to three of her relations, and it w as at lust determined by them that Zurbano and his brother in law should retire to a lonely grange, near the neighbouring village of Urtigosa. Here they remained secreted upu'ardsol a month, a few triends ministering to their wants. But a persevering and cunning partisan-chief followed þÿZurbano strack with the instinct of a bloodhound. Til's individual had, in duys of yore, beeo one of Zurbuno's smuggling companions, and alterwards a Cat list guerilla chief, not uncelebrated for his stiatagems and audacious enterprises, until he passed over to the Ghrislinos, a short time before the termination of the civil war, and was rewarded for

his treason with the rank ol major in the Spanish army. It appears that he had an idea that Zurbano was still lurking in the neighbourhood <d Logrono and Soria, and< urged on by the hope of rewaid and promo lion, Juan Mateo, or El Rayo. did not, like the commandants of the Queen's troops, give up the pursuit, but day and night continued his excursions and espionage, until he actually discovered the hiding place ot Zurbano and Cavatano Muro, El Rayo immediately hastened to the spot, with a few of tiis men and some soldiers which had been placed under his orders Gavatano .Vluro was the first who perceived the danger. He attempted to escape by leaping from a door in the hayloft, and was immediately killed hv a discharge of musketry. Zurbano was taken within the building. He made no resistance. On being led out. be beheld the yet warm body of his brother in law being strapped upon a mule, to be carried to Logrono. At this spectacle Zurbano ejaculated, Av de me I my pobrecuuado þÿ! (Alas ! my poor brotherinlaw!) He was likewise placed upon a rnuie, pinioned, and his feet tied to the animal's girth. In this plight, and surrounded by troops, whom the news of his capture had brought from the nearest post, Zurbnno was conveyed to the village of Tarquemada, and from thence to I.ogtono, where he was shot in the Plaza, in the presence ol some thousand spectators. Zurbano was the youngest son of a farmer of Barea, near Logrono. His father wished to make a priest of him, and he studied for
that vocation; hut as his conduct did not correspond with his þÿfather sviews, he was subsequently put to work on the farm. He married very young, and hired an extensive

farm, but becoming weary of that sort of life, he turned smuggler. He did not succeed in his new occupation, and got into embarrassment, which aflected the health of his wile, and she died. France possesses but little good steel, and what it has is made with foreign iron, and at a dear rate, on account of the þÿCustom s duties, which indiscriminately reaches iion suited for being converted into steel as well as iron unfit for such a purpose. From the day it was announced ihat an immense steam frigate was to be constructed hy Mr O Lang, the master shipwright of Woolwich dockyard, a ship superior to anything ever seen before in British waters was expected to he produced by everv nautical man who had witnessed the previous essays

of Mr Lang's genius and thorough practical knowledge. On Thursday, in the launch of the Terrible, iio one was disappointed, for a nobler vessel never breasted the wave or hoisted an ensign. Air. Lang had before shown his skill upon the Black Eagle, the Medea, the Plainer, <fcc., hut in the J errible lie has surpassed himself. In the words of a distinguished naval officer, who was present at the launch. þÿ " The Queen of England has now in her navy the first steamer in the world." This splendid steamer was commenced in November 1813. Her keel was laid on the 13ih of that month, consequently she lias been fourteen months and three weeks building, under the iinni. diate superintendence of Air. Lang, jon., and subsequently, on that gentleman's appointment to Chatham Dockyard, that of .Vlr. Wilcox. She has been constructed w.th gieat care, Air. Lang, her designer, having applied to her all the improvements which his long experience in naval construction has enabled him to introduce. leet 0 inches. Sec. 2. And be it further resolved. That the foregoing consent of Congress is given upon the following conditions, and with the following guarantees, to wit ;

First. Said Slate to be formed, subject to the adjustment by ibis government of all questions of boundary that may arise with otiier governments ; and the constitution thereof, with the proper evidence of its adoption by the people of said Republic ol lexas, shall be transmitted to the President ot the United Slates, to be laid before Congress lor its final action, on or before the first day of January, one thousand eight hundred and forty six Second, Said State, w hen admitted into the Union, alter ceding to the United Sta < s all mines, minerals, salt lakes and springs, and also all public edifices, fortifications, barracks, ports and harbours, navy and navy yards, docks, magazines, arms, armaments, and all other properly and means peitaining to the public defence belonging to said republic of Texas, shall retain all the public funds, debts, taxes and dues of every kind which may belong to, or be due and owing said republic ; and shall also retain ail the vacant and unappropriated lands lying within its limits to be applied to the payment ot the debts and liabilities of said republic of Texas ; and the residue of said lands, after discharging said debts tind liabilities, to be disposed of as said State may direct ; but in no event are said debts and liabilities io become a charge upon the government of llie United Slates. entitled to admission under the provisions of the federal constitution. And such Slates as may be formed out of that portion of said territory lying south ol 36 degrees 80 minutes north latitude, commonly known as the Missouri compromise line, shall be admitted into the Union, with or without slavery, as the people of each State asking admission may desire. The following is Mr. Walker's amendment, the same in substance as Mr. Benton's, except that it leaves the matter discretionary with the President to open negociations or not. March, 4, 145 To Texas the reunion is important, because the strong protecting arm ol our government would be extended over her, and the vast resources of her fertile sod and genial climate would fie speedily developed; while the safety of New Orleans and of our whole southwestern frontier against hostile aggression, as well as the interests of the whole Union, would he promoted by it. in the earlier stages of our national existence, the opinion prevailed with some, that our system of confederated States could tot opetate successfully over an extended territory, and Serious objections have, at different times, been made to the enlargement of our boundaries. These objections were earnestly urged when we acquired Louisiana FIxperienee has shown that they were not well founded. The title of numerous Indian tribes to vast tracts of country has been extinguished. þÿ New slates have been admitted into lite Union; new territories have been created, and our jurisdiction and laws extended over them. As our population has expanded, the Union has heert cemented and strengthened : as our boundaries have been enlarged, and our agricultural population lias been spread over a large surface, our fedeiative system lias acquired additional strength and security. It may well lie doubted whether n would not be in greater danger of overthrow ii our present population were confined to ihe comparatively narrow limits of the original thirteen Stales, than it is, now that they

are settled over a nioie expanded territory. It is confidently believed that our system may be safely extended to the utmost bounds of our territorial limits ; and that, as it shall be extended, the bonds of our Union, so far from being weakened, will be stronger. None can fail to see the danger to our safety and future peace, if Texas remains aa independent state, or becomes an ally or dependency of some foreign naiion more powerful than herself. Is there one among our citizens who would not prefer perpetual peace with Texas, to occasional wars, which so often occur between bur deiing independent nations ? Is there one who would not prefer free intercourse with tier, to high duties on nil our products and manufactuies which enter her pons or cross her frontiers? Is llieie one who would not prefer an unrestricted communication with her citizens, to ike frontier obstructions which must occur if she remains out of the Union ? Whatever is good or evil in the local institutions of Texas, will remain her own whether annexed to the United Slates or not. None of the present slates will be responsible fur them, any more than they are for the local institutions of each other. They have confederated together for certain specified objects. Upon the sitme principle that they would refuse to form a perpetual union with Texas because of Iter loca' institutions, our forefathers would have been prevented from forming our present Union. Perceiving no valid objection to the measure, and many reasons for its adopti n
vitally ailecting the peace, the safely and the prosperity of both countries, 1 shall, on the broad principle which formed the bat-is ai d produced the adoption ol our constitution..
